facts.text: Turkish red pine has thick bark, so fires that burn along the ground do it little harm.
Smoke in a forest or field is worth reporting, however small. Keep your distance and call 112.
Around the Mediterranean the dry summer can run from June to October, with almost no rain.
Fire usually moves faster uphill than downhill or on flat ground.
Wind feeds a fire fresh oxygen and pushes it toward new fuel, which makes it one of the main drivers of fire behaviour.
Clouds, thick smoke or tree canopy can hide a fire from a satellite. No detection does not mean no fire.
A fire can start and end between two overpasses, and then no satellite records it.
Some fires are too small or not hot enough for a satellite to detect.
A satellite hot spot is not always a vegetation fire; it can be a volcano or a gas flare.
Satellite fire data reaches NASA's fire map within about three hours of the overpass, so the map can be a few hours behind.
Aqua orbits Earth in about 99 minutes.
Fires start, grow and spread more easily in hot, dry and windy weather.
Embers can travel for kilometres and start new fires. A fire that looks distant can still reach you; follow official warnings.
At harvest time, sparks from harvesting machines can start fires. Machine maintenance reduces the risk.
Smoke from burning field stubble can reduce visibility on roads and has caused traffic accidents.
facts.source_name: Şanlıurfa Provincial Directorate of Agriculture and Forestry
